analysis.one_liner: Taxes coal, oil, and natural gas and rebates the money to every lawful resident.
analysis.headline: A carbon tax bill that paid every lawful resident a quarterly rebate was introduced in December 2015, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill put a fee on producing or importing coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide and rising $15 each year. Producers and importers paid the tax. Nearly all the money collected was sent back to lawful U.S. residents in equal quarterly payments, and goods imported from countries without a similar carbon price were charged an equivalent fee so foreign producers could not undercut American firms. The tax ended once U.S. emissions fell to half their 2005 level.
analysis.who_benefits: Lawful U.S. residents with a valid Social Security number receive an equal share of the carbon tax revenue every quarter. Because wealthier households use far more energy, an equal per-person rebate means most low- and middle-income households come out ahead even after paying higher fuel prices. It also pushes energy use toward cleaner sources, and renewable energy producers gain as fossil fuels become relatively more expensive.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low- and middle-income households receiving equal rebates

how_it_helps.text: Splits the entire carbon tax revenue into equal quarterly payments to every lawful resident with a valid Social Security number, so households that use less energy than average receive more in rebates than they pay in higher fuel prices.

Starts the tax at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide in 2016 and raises it $15 per year, steadily discouraging fossil fuel use until U.S. emissions fall to half their 2005 level, after which the annual increase stops.

Charges a carbon equivalency fee on imported goods from countries without an equivalent carbon price, protecting American manufacturers and workers from losing out to producers in countries that do not tax carbon.
Exempts exports from the tax so American fossil fuel producers and exporters are not disadvantaged in foreign markets.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers pay the tax, and they would pass some of the cost through to prices for gasoline, electricity, heating, and carbon-intensive goods. Households that use the most energy — larger homes, long commutes, energy-heavy businesses — pay more in higher prices than they receive back in rebates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and gas producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: The tax starts at $15 per ton and climbs $15 every year without a cap, so energy prices would rise sharply over time; households that use unusually large amounts of energy, such as rural drivers and families with high heating bills, could pay more than they get back, at least early on.
Rebates only go to people with valid Social Security numbers who are lawfully present, so some residents are taxed through higher prices but receive no rebate.

From 2027 the total rebate amount is capped at the 2026 average rather than the current year's collections, so if collections rise later, the difference stays in the Treasury instead of reaching households.

Enforcement depends on the Treasury Secretary estimating life-cycle emissions and setting equivalency fees on imported goods, a complicated and potentially litigious task that could be gamed or applied unevenly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is the classic carbon dividend: a rising price on fossil fuels paired with an equal refund to every resident, which shields most low- and middle-income households from the price increases while cutting emissions. The main honest concerns are the fast annual escalation, the exclusion of some residents from rebates, and the administrative complexity of the import fee. It was never estimated, amended, or debated in committee, so its practical effects were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced in December 2015, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on December 17, 2015 and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
The bill never advanced past that referral: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no action of any kind after the referral, according to its complete action history.
It drew only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers, who avoided a rising excise tax that took effect January 1, 2017 under the bill's terms; consumers also avoided the pass-through price increases, but forfeited the quarterly rebates and the emissions reductions the bill aimed for.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, spared a rising tax

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the carbon tax and rebate bill on December 17, 2015.

for.name: Two House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors to the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No one ever voted on the bill or spoke against it on the record; all three supporters were Democrats, so opposition was never measured, only implied by the bill going nowhere.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and importers
industries.note: The bill taxes their products at $15 per ton of carbon dioxide, rising $15 each year, with only exports exempt. They would bear the tax directly and pass much of it to consumers, so their interest was in keeping the bill from advancing — which is what happened.
A rising tax on coal, oil, and gas makes wind, solar, and other low-carbon energy relatively cheaper, growing their market as households and utilities shift away from fossil fuels.
The carbon equivalency fee charges imports from countries without a carbon price the same cost the tax imposes on American producers, keeping foreign competitors from undercutting U.S. factories.
